Our guide reminded us to stay quiet and [2] our binoculars carefully towards the tall reeds near the pond. Before long, a bright blue kingfisher landed on a branch, [3] made everyone smile. questions.explanation: 'Yet' introduces a contrast between expecting to need the countryside and counting twenty-three species inside a city park.
'Aim binoculars towards' means to point them in a particular direction; 'push' and 'reach' do not fit.

parts.title: Text cohesion: Dawn bird count

parts.title: Opinion matching: Wildlife in the city
parts.instructions: Four people (A-D) give their opinions about watching birds and protecting wildlife in towns and cities. Match each statement (1-7) to the correct person. You can use each person more than once.

texts.title: Ananya
texts.text: I live on the fourth floor of an apartment block, yet my tiny balcony has become a busy stop for city birds. Two years ago I hung up a simple seed feeder and placed a shallow dish of fresh water beside my herbs. Now robins and finches visit every morning while I drink my coffee. You do not need a large back garden to support local wildlife; even a single window box makes a difference.

texts.title: Callum
texts.text: People often complain that city parks look messy when councils stop cutting the grass in summer. Honestly, I think leaving wildflower strips around the edges of playing fields is one of the smartest changes our town has made. Within one season, bees, butterflies, and seed-eating birds returned in huge numbers. Still, I wish dog owners would keep their pets on leads near the pond where waterbirds build their nests.

texts.title: Ruby
texts.text: I started birdwatching last winter after downloading a free phone app that recognises bird songs from a short recording. Before that, every tweet in the park sounded identical to me! Now I can identify blackbirds, tits, and woodpeckers just by listening on my walk to the station. Watching wildlife has also helped me slow down and notice the changing seasons instead of rushing past trees without looking up.

texts.title: Tariq
texts.text: As a keen amateur photographer, I love the challenge of spotting foxes, herons, and owls inside our city. Unlike countryside animals, urban birds are often used to people walking nearby, so you can observe them clearly without expensive zoom lenses. That said, I never share the exact street location of a nest online, because too many visitors crowding round one tree can frighten young birds away.

parts.title: Long text comprehension: Wild neighbours in the city
parts.instructions: Read the article about how wild birds and animals adapt to modern cities. Match each paragraph (1-7) to the best heading (A-H). There is one extra heading that you do not need.

paragraphs.text: When most people picture wild animals, they imagine distant forests, open meadows, or quiet coastlines far away from traffic. Yet modern towns and cities are home to a surprising variety of wildlife. Red foxes trot along quiet residential streets after midnight, hedgehogs hunt for beetles under garden fences, and hawks nest on tall office roofs. Instead of disappearing as cities grew, many adaptable species learned to treat brick buildings, railway banks, and public parks as new kinds of habitat.

Birds in particular have found clever ways to make use of urban architecture. High stone ledges on churches and office towers closely resemble natural cliff faces, giving pigeons, swifts, and peregrine falcons safe places to raise chicks away from ground predators. Meanwhile, sheltered roofs and warm air vents help small birds survive freezing winter nights. Scientists studying city pigeons and starlings have even noticed that urban birds tend to wake earlier than their countryside cousins to beat morning traffic noise.

Noise is not the only challenge that city animals face when living alongside millions of people. Bright street lamps and illuminated shop windows can confuse migrating birds flying overhead at night, drawing them off course. In addition, wide glass windows often reflect sky and trees, making birds fly straight into the glass by mistake. Fortunately, simple steps such as switching off empty office lights after ten o'clock and adding faint patterns to large glass panels can prevent thousands of accidents.

Food is another major reason why wild creatures settle in towns, though human food is not always healthy for them. While parks and gardens provide natural berries, worms, and insects, discarded chips and bread offer very little nutrition. Ducklings fed too much white bread, for example, can develop weak wings, and leftover bread rots in ponds and harms water quality. Wildlife charities therefore encourage families to feed ducks oats, peas, or sweetcorn instead of old loaves.

Across many countries, city planners are now designing greener neighbourhoods that welcome both people and wildlife. Small concrete corners are being turned into pocket gardens planted with native flowers, while canals and rivers are cleaned up so otters and kingfishers can return. Even small gaps cut into the bottom of wooden garden fences create 'hedgehog highways', allowing small mammals to travel safely between yards in search of food without crossing busy roads.

At the same time, ordinary residents are helping scientists track how urban wildlife is changing. Every winter and spring, thousands of families spend an hour counting the birds in their street or park and sending the numbers to national databases. This community data reveals which species are thriving and which ones need extra help. For instance, falling sparrow numbers in several cities led local groups to plant thicker hedges where small birds can hide and nest.

For city dwellers, noticing local birds and animals brings clear benefits to everyday life. Listening to a blackbird sing outside a kitchen window or watching ducks cross a canal during a lunch break offers a brief, calming connection to the natural world. You do not need expensive travel or specialist gear to start birdwatching; a quiet bench, a little patience, and curiosity are enough to turn any neighbourhood walk into a small discovery.

headings: How citizens help researchers monitor local species
Why tall buildings suit certain nesting birds
Choosing safer food for park waterbirds
Simple design changes that connect city habitats
Surprising wildlife living right beside urban streets
How artificial light and glass create hidden dangers
Training rescue dogs to find injured hedgehogs
Everyday rewards of noticing nature near home

gaps.explanation: Paragraph 1 introduces how foxes, hedgehogs, and hawks live in towns and treat city spaces as habitats.
Paragraph 2 explains how tall stone ledges resemble cliffs for nesting birds and warm buildings help them survive winter.
Paragraph 3 describes how bright night lights confuse migrating birds and reflective glass windows cause collisions.
Paragraph 4 explains why bread harms ducks and ponds, and recommends oats, peas, or sweetcorn instead.
Paragraph 5 describes pocket gardens, cleaner canals, and fence gaps ('hedgehog highways') that connect urban habitats.
Paragraph 6 explains how residents count birds in their streets and send data to help scientists track species.
Paragraph 7 focuses on how noticing local birds brings calm and connection to daily city life without expensive travel.

parts.title: Monologue comprehension
parts.instructions: Listen to two speakers giving short talks: first an ecologist about installing bird boxes on city buildings (questions 1-2), then a volunteer about rescuing injured garden hedgehogs (questions 3-4). Choose the best answer for each question.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: First, you will hear Ananya, an urban wildlife researcher, talking about putting special nesting boxes on modern city buildings.

turns.speaker: ananya
turns.text: When our team began putting wooden nesting boxes for swifts on city apartment blocks, people often asked why birds could not just nest in park trees. The truth is that swifts spend almost their entire lives in the air and prefer high gaps under roofs. Older brick houses used to have plenty of tiny spaces under the roof tiles, whereas modern glass-and-steel buildings are sealed completely tight. So adding simple nesting boxes just below the roof line replaces those lost homes. We expected young couples living in the flats to enjoy watching the birds return each May. What really surprised us, though, was how many retired residents started keeping daily notebooks on when the chicks hatched and sharing updates in the building lobby. Turning a plain grey apartment wall into something neighbours talk about warmly has been the most rewarding part of our work.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Now you will hear George, a wildlife volunteer, talking about helping hedgehogs in town gardens.

turns.speaker: george
turns.text: People often imagine that volunteering at a hedgehog rescue centre means cuddling cute animals in warm blankets all afternoon. In reality, most of our work involves cleaning cages, weighing tiny patients, and answering worried phone calls from garden owners. The hardest part for me isn't waking up early for feeding times — it's seeing how many injuries are caused by everyday garden mistakes, such as strimmers cutting tall grass or plastic netting left on the ground. Whenever homeowners ask me how they can help hedgehogs right away, I tell them not to buy fancy wooden houses first. Instead, simply cut a small square hole at the bottom of your garden fence so hedgehogs can walk safely between yards at night without crossing busy streets.

1. What are the advantages of watching birds outdoors with binoculars compared with watching birds at a garden feeder?
2. Which of these two activities would you prefer to do on a weekend morning, and why?

parts.title: Personal experience and discussion
parts.instructions: You have 1 minute to prepare and 2 minutes to speak continuously. Answer all three questions in one organised talk.

topics.prompt:
Talk about a time when you saw an interesting wild bird or animal. Answer all three questions in one 2-minute talk:
1. Tell me about a time when you saw a wild bird or animal in a park, garden, or countryside.
2. How did you feel when you noticed it, and what did you do?
3. Why do you think protecting wild animals and birds inside modern cities is important?
